cards.title: Addressing Mexican Air Force
cards.body: Mexican air force ranks are similar to US ranks. Use formal titles (e.g., 'Coronel', 'Teniente') followed by surname. For civilians, use 'Señor' or 'Señora' with surname. Handshakes are common, but wait for senior personnel to initiate.
doThis: Wait for seniors to initiate contact
avoidThis: Interrupting or speaking out of turn

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints and Security
cards.body: Checkpoints are common. Always carry ID. Be polite and patient. If refused entry, do not argue. Instead, ask for clarification and follow instructions. Use 'por favor' and 'gracias' to maintain good relations.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Respect Hierarchy in Mexico
cards.body: Mexican culture values hierarchy and respect for seniors. Use formal titles and last names when addressing superiors. Wait for invitations to use first names.
doThis: Address seniors as 'Señor' or 'Señora' followed by their last name.
Wait for permission to use first names.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Refusals Politely
cards.body: Mexicans often avoid direct refusal to maintain politeness. 'Ahorita' means 'not now, maybe later'. Be patient and indirect when declining offers.
avoidThis: Rush or pressure for immediate answers.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Mexico
cards.body: Mexican culture values hierarchy and respect for seniors. Use formal titles and last names initially, then switch to first names if invited. Avoid direct disagreement with superiors.
doThis: Use 'Señor', 'Señora', or professional titles with last names

cards.title: Navigating Refusal and Criticism
cards.body: Mexicans often avoid direct refusal or criticism to maintain harmony. They may use indirect language or explanations instead of a straightforward 'no'. Be patient and understanding.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Mexico
cards.body: Mexicans value hierarchy and formal titles. Use titles like 'Señor,' 'Señora,' or professional titles with last names. For elders or high-status individuals, use 'Don' or 'Doña' with the first name.
doThis: Use formal titles when addressing seniors
Maintain eye contact to show respect
avoidThis: Standing too far away during conversations

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Saving Face in Mexico
cards.body: Mexicans avoid direct criticism or rejection to maintain harmony. Speak indirectly and use explanations instead of saying 'no.' Avoid public disagreements or confrontations.
doThis: Provide explanations instead of direct refusals

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints in Mexico
cards.body: Checkpoints are common in Mexico. Be patient and polite. Have required documents ready. Follow instructions from security staff.

cards.title: Respect Hierarchy and Titles
cards.body: Mexican military culture emphasizes rank. Address seniors with their rank and last name, like 'Coronel García.' For civilians, use 'Señor' or 'Señora' with their last name. Avoid first names unless invited.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names
Wait for permission to use first names

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Navigate Disagreements Tactfully
cards.body: Mexicans value harmony. Express disagreements privately, indirectly, and politely. Use 'perhaps' or 'maybe' to soften criticism. Avoid public confrontation to save face.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Respect for Religious Elders
cards.body: Mexican culture values respect for elders and religious figures. Address seniors with formal titles and show deference. Be mindful of Catholic influences in daily life and traditions.
doThis: Use formal titles (e.g., 'Señor', 'Doctor') when addressing seniors
Show respect for religious figures and traditions
avoidThis: Show overt signs of disinterest during religious events

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Religious Differences
cards.body: While Mexico is predominantly Catholic, there are diverse beliefs. Avoid religious debates and respect individual practices. Be mindful of Catholic holidays and traditions.
doThis: Acknowledge and respect diverse religious beliefs
Learn about major Catholic holidays and their significance
Be open to participating in religious events respectfully

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Gifts for Seniors: Hierarchy Matters
cards.body: Mexican air force personnel value hierarchy. When giving gifts, consider rank. Gifts are often exchanged to show respect and appreciation. Choose thoughtful, modest gifts like local delicacies, or items that represent your home state or country.
doThis: Address seniors with their rank and last name.
Give gifts with both hands as a sign of respect.
avoidThis: Give overly expensive or extravagant gifts.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Gifts and Face: Be Tactful
cards.body: Mexicans value 'saving face'. Avoid public criticism or disagreement. If you must refuse a gift or request, do so politely and privately. Use indirect language to soften the refusal.
doThis: Use polite, indirect language when refusing.
Give and receive gifts with a smile and warm words.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Meals
cards.body: Mexican military culture values hierarchy. Seniors are addressed first and served first. Wait for seniors to begin eating. Use formal titles like 'Señor' or 'Teniente' followed by their last name. Avoid interrupting or contradicting seniors during meals.
doThis: Wait for seniors to start eating

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Meal Refusals
cards.body: Mexicans often avoid direct refusal to be polite. 'Ahorita' means 'not now, but maybe later.' If you must refuse, do so gently. Avoid abrupt or direct refusals, which can cause offense. Offer alternatives if possible.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Meetings
cards.body: Mexican military and business structures are hierarchical. Address seniors with their rank and last name. Wait for them to initiate more casual interactions. In meetings, decisions come from the top.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names for seniors
Wait for seniors to suggest familiarity
avoidThis: Using first names with seniors unless invited
Disagreeing openly with seniors in meetings

cards.title: Navigating Base Checkpoints
cards.body: Security checkpoints are common. Carry ID at all times. Be polite and patient. Understand that locals may have different access rules. Follow instructions carefully.

cards.title: Respecting Rank in Radio
cards.body: Mexican air force personnel value hierarchy. Use formal titles and last names for seniors, like 'Señor Comandante' or 'Señora Coronel'. For civilians, 'Señor' or 'Señora' with their last name is respectful. Avoid using first names unless invited.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names for seniors
Address civilians respectfully with 'Señor' or 'Señora' and their last name
Wait for permission to use first names

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Mexico (2025)

cards.title: Radio Etiquette in Mexico
cards.body: Mexicans prefer indirect communication to save face. Be polite and patient on the radio. Avoid criticism or disagreement openly. If you must refuse, explain gently and avoid a direct 'no'. Use phrases like 'No es posible' (It's not possible) or 'No estoy seguro' (I'm not sure).
doThis: Be polite and patient on the radio
